text: The data's connected and shaped. Before dragging a single visual onto a Power BI page, we're going to sketch the layout — the same discipline that paid off when we planned the query before writing SQL.

Three visuals cover this requirement completely. Two KPI cards up top — total sales amount and total order count — answer how are we doing, overall, in the first half second of looking at the page. A bar chart shows total sales by territory, answering which regions are driving sales. And a table holds the full detail — territory, product line, sales, and orders — for anyone who wants to dig one level deeper.

Notice what's missing. No line chart, because there's no trend to show — this report covers one quarter, not a series of periods, so a chart built for change over time wouldn't fit the data. And no pie chart — with several territories and several product lines, a pie would either hide detail or turn into an unreadable wedge of slices.

Sketch the page as a rough grid before opening Power BI at all. KPI cards across the top. Underneath, the bar chart on the left and the table on the right. This sketch is the plan for the next two lessons — DAX measures to power the cards and the chart, then slicers and formatting to finish the page.

One more choice worth explaining: a flat table, not a matrix, for the detail view. A matrix is for pivoting two dimensions into rows and columns. A flat table is simpler for a stakeholder to scan, and it matches the shape the T-SQL query already produces — one row per territory and product line combination.
With the layout sketched, next lesson we write the DAX measures that will actually power these cards and this chart — total sales, and order count, explained clearly from scratch.
